strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored question—characterizing the connectivity/geometry of the full-dimensional low-loss region rather than only pairwise mode connectivity—which extends prior AutoNEB/mode-connectivity literature.

Experiments span three distinct architectures (LeNet5, ResNet18, CCT7) and additional models in the appendix (MobileNetV2, ShuffleNet, ResNet18@CIFAR100), showing some generality of the proposed path-finding procedure.

The comparison against AutoNEB is a useful quantitative anchor: the proposed LLPF algorithm reaches a lower maximum loss threshold (0.006) than AutoNEB's reported minimum (0.016) on a similar ResNet setting, providing some evidence of stronger connectivity.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility documentation: detailed hyperparameter tables (Tables 1–6), computation time reporting, and explicit description of preprocessing/augmentation.

The 'variance sphere' framing and the model-to-origin algorithm offer an intuitive and novel visualization/exploration tool, and the PCA layer-wise visualization (Figure 4, Figure 9) is a creative diagnostic idea.
The observed generalization improvement from moving pretrained ImageNet1k ResNet18 weights toward the origin (69.76%→70.55%) is a potentially practically interesting finding if it replicates.
weaknesses: The central claim that the low-loss space is 'continuous and fully connected' is a strong topological assertion, but the evidence only demonstrates that pairs of points obtained from independently trained models under identical hyperparameters/architecture can be connected by an algorithmically constructed path. This is a much weaker property than full connectedness of the level set defined in Eq. 1, and the paper does not clearly justify why connecting sampled pairs generalizes to the entire low-loss space (e.g., no argument or test for points far from the SGD-trained-model manifold, adversarially chosen points, or points from different training regimes/pruned models).

The algorithm requires substantial architecture-specific, hand-tuned scheduling (layer-by-layer phases with different step sizes and orderings, as seen in Table 1, and different configurations needed for VGG16 without batchnorm), undermining the claim of a general, algorithm-agnostic phenomenon; the 'prerequisites' section admits the method fails for sharp minima (e.g., Adam-trained ResNet18), which is a common and important training regime.

The 'no redundant parameters in the low-loss space' claim (Section 5, contribution 3) is supported only by a vaguely described SVD analysis ('we construct multiple low-loss paths... via a single training iteration with large batch size') with no quantitative figure, table, singular-value spectrum, or statistical test provided in the paper; this is a strong and somewhat counter-intuitive claim (given extensive pruning/lottery-ticket literature) that needs much more rigorous empirical support than a qualitative assertion.

Generalization-improvement experiments (Figure 5) are based on single or few runs without repeated trials, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing, especially for the headline ImageNet1k result (+0.8% accuracy), making it hard to rule out noise; no baseline comparison against simply adding weight decay or L2 regularization with matched compute is provided to isolate the specific benefit of the proposed traversal.

Several core approximations (zero mean of weights, similarity of variance spheres across seeds, Eq. 4/5) are validated empirically only for ResNet18, not for LeNet5, CCT7, or the additional architectures in Appendix A.4, weakening the generality of the theoretical framework underlying the algorithms.

The abstract/title make broad claims ('Low-Loss Space in Neural Networks is Continuous and Fully Connected') that are considerably stronger than what the restricted, per-architecture-tuned, empirically-limited experiments actually establish; the paper's own admission that the space is bounded (the origin is not low-loss) and that normalization layers must be excluded from Algorithm 2 further qualifies the 'fully connected' narrative in ways not reflected in the title.

The computational cost of the proposed algorithms is very high (e.g., 340 GPU-hours for the ImageNet1k experiment, 24–48 GPU-hours per single ResNet18/CCT7 run), which is not discussed as a limitation relative to the practical utility of the proposed generalization-improvement application.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation overload and some inconsistent algorithm line references (e.g., Table 2 refers to 'A1 L4' for what is described as Algorithm 2), which could hinder reproducibility despite the otherwise fairly complete hyperparameter tables.

strengths: The paper investigates an interesting and underexplored question: whether low-loss regions in parameter space form a globally connected structure, extending beyond prior pairwise mode-connectivity results.
The experimental scope is reasonably broad, covering LeNet5, ResNet18, and CCT7, with additional architectures (MobileNet, ShuffleNet) in the appendix.
Extensive hyperparameter tables and algorithmic pseudocode are provided, which aids partial reproducibility even though no code release is mentioned.
The PCA-based layer-wise visualization of low-loss paths is a novel and potentially useful diagnostic tool for qualitatively inspecting representational sharpness per layer.
The practical demonstration of using Algorithm 2 to slightly improve a pretrained ResNet18 on ImageNet1k is an interesting applied angle, even if not rigorously validated.
weaknesses: The central claim that the low-loss space is 'fully connected' as a single topological space is a strong, essentially global/topological statement, but the evidence offered is only a finite number of pairwise path constructions (200/40/10 repetitions per architecture) between models trained with identical hyperparameters. This is an inductive leap that does not constitute proof of full connectivity in the rigorous sense used in the abstract and title, and is not meaningfully different in kind from prior empirical mode-connectivity works (e.g., AutoNEB, Garipov et al.), which the paper claims to go beyond.

The 'no redundant parameters in the low-loss space' claim (Section 5) rests on an SVD dimensionality argument that is statistically weak: for a modest number of sampled directions in a very high-dimensional space, near-full-rank spanning is close to guaranteed for generic vectors regardless of any true low-dimensional structure or redundancy (e.g., known symmetries such as permutation/scaling invariances). The argument does not actually rule out redundancy and conflates 'local low-loss directions exist in most coordinates' with 'the low-loss space has full-D dimensionality with no redundant parameters,' which is a much stronger and unsupported claim.

The comparison with AutoNEB is not apples-to-apples: the paper compares its own ResNet18/CIFAR10 loss values against numbers reported in a different paper for a different architecture (ResNet20) under different conditions (Table B.1 of [8]), rather than re-running AutoNEB under identical settings. This undermines the claimed quantitative superiority.

Key experimental design choices lack statistical rigor: the number of repetitions varies drastically across architectures (200 vs. 40 vs. 10), no confidence intervals, significance tests, or ablations are reported to support claims of 'consistency' beyond qualitative visual inspection of shaded regions in plots.

The ImageNet1k generalization result (69.758% -> 70.55%) is based on a single run with no repeated trials, no comparison against simply increasing weight decay/regularization strength (which the paper itself notes is conceptually similar to moving toward the origin), and no analysis of the extra compute cost incurred, making it hard to assess whether this is a genuinely new mechanism or a re-derivation of standard regularization effects via a more expensive route.

Several foundational definitions (e.g., 'Flat Low-Loss Region', prerequisites for Algorithm 1/2) are described only informally by reference to figures in other papers rather than given precise, checkable criteria, weakening the theoretical rigor of a paper that positions itself as making 'foundational' contributions to neural network theory.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, which combined with the many architecture-specific, hand-tuned, multi-phase hyperparameter schedules (Table 1, layer-by-layer ordering) raises concerns about practical reproducibility of the specific results despite the detailed hyperparameter tables.

The framing of contributions (e.g., 'we conclude the low-loss space constitutes a fully-connected space,' 'no parameter is redundant in defining it') significantly overstates what the empirical evidence can support, which is a soundness concern rather than a purely presentational one.

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely novel algorithmic contribution (LLPF_M2M and LLPF_M2O) that extends beyond simple two-point mode-connectivity approaches (e.g., AutoNEB, polynomial interpolation) by explicitly modeling the 'variance sphere' concept and constructing paths in the full parameter space rather than only between two fixed endpoints.

Experiments span multiple architectures (LeNet5, ResNet18, CCT7) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR10/100, ImageNet1k), with additional architectures (MobileNetv2, ShuffleNet) tested in the appendix, showing some breadth.

The paper provides empirical validation of its own underlying approximations (Equations 3-5, validated in Appendix A.1-A.2 for ResNet18), which is good scientific practice and improves credibility of the method's assumptions.

Comparison against AutoNEB is informative, showing lower maximum loss along constructed paths, and the paper is reasonably transparent about hyperparameters, computation costs (Table 5), and architecture-specific configurations, aiding partial reproducibility.

The practical application to improve ImageNet1k ResNet18 test accuracy (69.758% -> 70.55%) via moving toward the origin is an interesting, potentially useful empirical finding connecting the low-loss space geometry to generalization.

The PCA-based visualization of low-loss paths (Figure 4, 9) offers a novel diagnostic angle on per-layer feature sensitivity, tentatively linking sharper visual patterns in early conv layers to loss landscape sharpness.
weaknesses: The central claims that the low-loss space is 'continuous and fully connected' as a single topological space are considerably stronger than what the evidence supports: the experiments only show that specific pairs of models trained under identical hyperparameters (same variance sphere) can be connected by the proposed constructive algorithm. This does not establish full connectivity of the entire low-loss space, nor rule out disconnected components reachable only from different training setups, sharper minima, or different architectures; the title's strong universal claim is not adequately hedged relative to the narrower empirical scope.

The claim that the low-loss space has 'no redundant parameters' (derived from an SVD rank argument on single-step training directions) is under-motivated and possibly conflates dimensionality of locally-spanned directions with the established notion of parameter redundancy from pruning/lottery-ticket literature. The paper's reconciliation of this with prior over-parameterization findings is a semantic reframing rather than a rigorous theoretical or empirical bridge, and risks overclaiming a foundational-sounding but weakly supported result.

The algorithm requires careful, architecture-specific, manually staged application to specific subsets of layers in a specific order (Appendix Table 1, 2, 6), with different step sizes and iteration counts per phase. This heavy manual tuning undermines the generality and practical reproducibility of the method, and it is unclear how a new user would derive the correct layer ordering/schedule for an unseen architecture without extensive trial and error.

Key results rely on very limited repetition for larger-scale settings: ResNet18@CIFAR100 and ResNet18@ImageNet1k generalization improvements (Figure 5) appear to be based on a single run each, with no reported variance or multiple seeds, despite the ImageNet1k experiment requiring 340 GPU-hours — this makes the headline generalization improvement difficult to verify as statistically robust rather than a one-off fluctuation.

The prerequisite that starting points must lie in 'flat' minima (with ResNet18 trained via Adam explicitly failing as a counterexample) suggests the demonstrated connectivity is conditional on a favorable, possibly cherry-picked training regime (SGD without momentum/weight decay for the path-finding phase), which weakens the generality of the continuity/connectedness claim across common training setups.

The related work and comparisons are largely limited to the 2018 AutoNEB paper and mode-connectivity work from a similar era; more recent literature on neural network mode connectivity, permutation symmetry (git re-basin style methods), and loss landscape geometry is not discussed or compared against, leaving the positioning of the contribution relative to the current state of the art incomplete.

Presentation issues (dense notation, some inconsistent algorithmic references, minor typographical errors such as stray periods and inconsistent capitalization) somewhat hinder readability, and several theoretical derivations (e.g., Equation 6) rely on approximations validated only for ResNet18, not for LeNet5 or CCT7 where the same assumptions are used.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: prior mode-connectivity methods (AutoNEB, FGE, SPRO) were validated mainly on older architectures (basic CNNs, VGG, ResNet, DenseNet), and this paper extends empirical study to a much broader and more modern set of architectures (MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, CCT).

Provides a reasonably careful conceptual framework (variance spheres, low-loss space, layer-wise decomposition) to motivate why layer-wise treatment should help, and empirically checks the underlying approximations (Appendix A.1, A.2) at least for ResNet-18.

Extensive experimental breadth: results are shown for many architectures/datasets in the main text and appendix, with repeated trials (>=10) to support reproducibility claims, and clear reporting of hyperparameters/settings for replication.
Novel exploration of connecting modes obtained with different training hyperparameters (different variance spheres), a setting not previously evaluated by prior mode-connectivity work.
Honest and specific limitations section that identifies the lack of generalization/test-loss guarantees along the discovered paths rather than glossing over it.
Reasonably reproducible: detailed hyperparameter tables, dataset preprocessing steps, and stated compute/hardware are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The method requires extensive, hand-crafted, per-architecture layer-ordering and multi-phase schedules (e.g., 21 phases for DLA, 8-9 phases for CCT7 in Table 2), which undercuts the claim of a general, broadly applicable algorithm; substantial manual engineering per architecture is needed even with the proposed FDF heuristic.

No direct, controlled head-to-head comparison with AutoNEB/FGE/SPRO on the same architectures/datasets; the comparison in Table 1 juxtaposes results from different papers on different model variants (ResNet-20 vs ResNet-158 vs ResNet-18), so the 'worst case training loss' and 'consistency' comparisons are not rigorous or apples-to-apples.

The algorithm optimizes only training loss and explicitly does not preserve test/generalization performance along the path (acknowledged in Limitations), which is a significant regression relative to prior methods like FGE/AutoNEB that the authors themselves note tend to preserve test performance—this weakens the practical significance of the contribution.

Computational cost is very high (Table 6 reports up to 45 hours on high-end GPUs, equivalent to tens/hundreds of thousands of training epochs), yet there is no systematic cost-accuracy comparison against baseline connectivity methods, making it hard to judge whether the improved 'consistency' and lower worst-case loss are worth the overhead.

Evidence for the 'different variance sphere' claim (connecting modes trained with different hyperparameters) is limited to varying weight decay in a small number of architectures (DLA in main text, ResNet18/CCT7 in appendix), which is a narrow test of a claimed core contribution.

Core theoretical claims (Equations 4 and 5, i.e., similar variance across independently trained modes and near-zero layer means) are empirically validated only for ResNet-18, yet used as a general justification/prerequisite for applying the method to structurally very different architectures (transformers, grouped convolutions, etc.).

All experiments are restricted to CIFAR-10/100 and MNIST; no evaluation at ImageNet or larger scale is provided, which limits the significance of claims about generalizing to 'modern' architectures that are typically used at larger scale.

The algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: layer-wise mode connectivity itself is attributed to prior work (Adilova et al., 2024), and the proposed method largely operationalizes this idea with variance-sphere projection and manually tuned schedules, rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

Presentation is heavy on formalism (variance spheres, geometric derivations) for procedures that are conceptually simple (move toward target, rescale variance, retrain), which may obscure rather than clarify the actual algorithmic contribution for readers.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in the mode-connectivity literature: prior algorithms (AutoNEB, FGE, SPRO) were validated mainly on older architectures (basic CNN, VGG, ResNet, DenseNet), and this paper attempts to extend empirical evidence to a wider and more modern set of architectures (MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, CCT).

Extensive empirical effort: experiments are repeated 10+ times per architecture/dataset pair to report consistency, and the appendix provides substantial supporting material (variance/mean validation across 100 independently trained ResNet-18 models, continuity checks via linear interpolation, timing/compute cost tables, full hyperparameter listings), which aids transparency.

Introduces and empirically demonstrates a new setting -- connecting modes trained with different hyperparameters (different "variance spheres") -- that prior mode-connectivity papers did not test, which is a modestly novel contribution.

Clear discussion distinguishing true independent-training mode connectivity from the related but distinct settings of model spawning and permutation, correcting a conflation present in some prior literature (e.g., re-examining the Garipov et al. ImageNet claim).
Code is stated to be included in supplementary material, supporting reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: The core algorithm requires extensive, architecture-specific and even phase-specific manual tuning (see Table 2: per-model, per-phase choices of layer subsets, step sizes, and training rounds), which undercuts the claim of a general, broadly applicable method; each new architecture appears to require bespoke engineering rather than an automated or principled procedure.

The comparison to prior work (Table 1) is not apples-to-apples: 'worst-case training loss' figures for AutoNEB/FGE/SPRO are taken from the original papers on different architectures/settings and explicitly noted as 'not strictly comparable,' so the central quantitative claim of superiority is not well supported by direct experiments under matched conditions.

The theoretical scaffolding (variance sphere, low-loss space, Eq. 4-6) rests on approximations (e.g., zero-mean assumption, proportionality between variance and squared distance) validated only on a single architecture (ResNet-18/CIFAR-10, Appendix A.1-A.2), yet is presented as a general justification across all tested architectures.

A major stated limitation is that LLPF does not preserve generalization/test performance along discovered paths (unlike AutoNEB/FGE, which the authors themselves note tend to find paths with good test behavior), which weakens the practical value of the contribution relative to prior methods for common downstream uses like ensembling.

Computational cost is very high relative to standard training (Table 6 reports up to 21-45 GPU-hours on H100/RTX5090 for a single connectivity path on CIFAR-scale models), raising concerns about scalability and practical significance, especially since evaluation is restricted to small datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10/100) despite claims about 'modern' architectures typically used at larger scale (e.g., ImageNet).

The paper does not report success/failure rates or clear quantitative consistency metrics (e.g., fraction of seed pairs for which the algorithm converges) beyond qualitative plots and verbal claims like 'validated via hundreds of simulations,' making the reproducibility/consistency claim hard to verify rigorously.

Loss thresholds defining 'low-loss' differ substantially and seemingly arbitrarily across architectures/tables (e.g., 0.006 vs 0.04 vs 0.05), without a principled or dataset-independent criterion, making cross-architecture claims of success difficult to compare or generalize.

The heavy, quasi-formal mathematical machinery (variance sphere definitions, derivations) is used to describe what is ultimately a fairly heuristic SGD + variance-renormalization procedure with manual layer ordering (FDF), creating a mismatch between apparent theoretical rigor and the actual ad hoc nature of the algorithm's design choices.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: prior mode-connectivity work (AutoNEB, FGE, SPRO) is confined to older architectures (CNN, VGG, ResNet, DenseNet), while this paper extends empirical mode-connectivity investigation to modern, structurally diverse networks (MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, CCT).

Extensive empirical evaluation across many architectures and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100), with results repeated 10+ times per setting to assess reproducibility of the discovered paths — a dimension prior papers largely ignored.

The variance-sphere formalization and layer-wise 'Follow Data Flow' ordering strategy provide a reasonably clear conceptual account of why naive full-parameter interpolation fails for complex/heterogeneous architectures, connecting to and extending the layer-wise linear mode connectivity literature (Adilova et al., 2024).

Novel demonstration that modes trained with different hyperparameters (and hence lying on different 'variance spheres') can be connected via a two-stage model-to-origin + model-to-model procedure — a setting not evaluated in prior mode-connectivity work.

Good transparency: detailed hyperparameter tables, dataset preprocessing details, computation-time tables, and additional continuity checks (linear interpolation between consecutive path points) are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
The limitations section is honest, correctly identifying that LLPF does not guarantee low test loss along the path, unlike loss-barrier-based methods such as AutoNEB/FGE.
weaknesses: The central comparison in Table 1 (worst-case training loss, 'consistency', architecture coverage) is not a controlled head-to-head comparison: baseline numbers are taken from the original papers on different architectures/datasets/training budgets, so claims of superior consistency and lower loss are not rigorously substantiated against the same experimental conditions; the paper itself acknowledges these losses 'are not strictly comparable across papers.'

The claim that LLPF 'generalizes beyond traditional architectures' rests partly on the (unverified) inference that prior methods would fail on these architectures — the paper does not actually run AutoNEB/FGE/SPRO on MobileNet/ShuffleNet/etc. to demonstrate their failure, so the comparative advantage is asserted rather than empirically demonstrated.

The method requires substantial architecture-specific manual engineering: Table 2 shows DLA needs 21 hand-crafted phases and CCT7 needs 8-9 phases with tuned per-phase hyperparameters, which undercuts the claim of a generally applicable algorithm and raises concerns about scalability to new/larger architectures without extensive tuning effort.

All experiments are restricted to small-scale datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10/100); no validation at ImageNet or larger scale is provided, limiting confidence that findings transfer to the regimes where these modern architectures (EfficientNet, RegNet, etc.) are typically used in practice.

The mathematical formalism (variance spheres, Equation 6 'proof') is largely elementary algebra dressed in heavy notation; it does not add rigor or a theoretical guarantee, and the core method remains a hand-tuned, layer-sequential SGD-based interpolation-with-variance-correction heuristic.

Reported computational costs are substantial in the worst case (up to ~45 hours on an RTX 5090 or H100 for a single mode connection), which is not clearly contextualized against the cost of prior methods, making practical significance harder to judge.

Reproducibility/consistency claims rely on visual inspection of mean±std curves across repetitions rather than a clearly defined quantitative success criterion or statistical test, making the 'consistent' label in Table 1 somewhat subjective.

The finding that Algorithm 1 does not preserve test performance (e.g., rising test loss for ResNet18 despite low training loss) is an important limitation that meaningfully narrows the practical usefulness of the discovered connections for generalization-oriented applications (e.g., ensembling).

strengths: Extensive empirical validation across a genuinely broad set of architectures (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, LeNet, MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, CCT) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR10/100, ImageNet10), going well beyond prior mode-connectivity work.

Valuable critical re-examination of prior methods: the paper identifies a concrete bug in the released FGE training script (fixed random seed causing near-identical initializations) and demonstrates via cosine-similarity analysis that FGE's reported 'independently trained' modes are actually highly correlated, and shows AutoNEB's high run-to-run variance (0.5–1.5 training loss) using the authors' own configs. This is a useful service to the community.

Thorough ablation studies (removing layer-wise moves, training steps, variance correction) and continuity checks (linear interpolation between consecutive path points) that support the internal validity of the proposed mechanism.

Reasonably detailed reproducibility documentation (extensive hyperparameter tables, dataset preprocessing steps, per-phase configurations in the appendix) and an honest discussion of limitations (test loss not guaranteed to track training loss, high computational cost, lack of theoretical grounding for the 'full path-connectedness' conjecture).

The variance-sphere/layer-wise perspective combined with a model-to-model and model-to-origin procedure is a sensible synthesis of existing ideas (layer-wise LMC, vanishing variance correction) that provides a practical mechanism for crossing between different training regimes (different hyperparameters).
weaknesses: The claim of 'generalizing beyond traditional architectures' is substantially undercut by the fact that success depends critically on manually chosen layer ordering and per-phase hyperparameters (Table 4 shows up to 20+ hand-crafted phases for DLA, distinct settings per architecture). This is closer to a flexible framework requiring substantial per-model engineering than an automatic, generalizable algorithm, which limits practical significance and ease of adoption by other researchers.

Extremely high computational cost (tens of hours on H100/RTX GPUs per single mode-pair connection, per Table 8) raises concerns about scalability and practical usability, especially since larger-scale (e.g., true ImageNet) experiments are explicitly excluded due to resource constraints.

Theoretical grounding is thin: key relationships (Equation 4's variance similarity across seeds, Equation 5's zero-mean approximation) are justified only empirically via a limited set of models, and the central claims (e.g., 'low-loss tunnels' connecting all SGD basins) remain speculative with no formal support, as acknowledged by the authors themselves.

The definition of 'low loss' / training-loss threshold is not fixed or principled; different experiments use different thresholds and stopping criteria, and the reported 'worst-case training loss' comparisons to AutoNEB/FGE (Table 1) use different network depths/architectures (ResNet18 vs ResNet20/ResNet158), making the quantitative comparison not fully apples-to-apples.

Test-set behavior along discovered paths is not reliably low-loss (e.g., ResNet18@CIFAR10 case shows increasing test loss despite low training loss), which limits the practical utility of the method for downstream applications such as ensembling or model merging, though this is honestly reported.

No direct quantitative comparison to the closely related layer-wise linear mode connectivity work (Adilova et al. 2024) that the method explicitly builds on, making it harder to isolate the specific algorithmic contribution beyond assembling known components (variance correction, layer-wise ordering, learning-rate scaling).

strengths: Extensive empirical study spanning many CNN and transformer-style architectures (ResNet, DenseNet, VGG, MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, CCT) beyond the narrow set typically used in mode-connectivity literature.

Careful and honest scrutiny of prior baselines: the paper identifies a concrete bug in the released FGE training script (fixed random seed causing near-identical initializations) and documents run-to-run inconsistency of AutoNEB with quantitative evidence (Tables 1, 9), which is a useful community contribution.

Substantial supplementary validation effort: reproducibility across repeated runs, linear-interpolation continuity checks between consecutive path points, ablations isolating the role of layer-wise movement, retraining, and variance correction, and an appendix example where LLPF succeeds where AutoNEB fails.
Demonstrates connectivity across different training hyperparameters (different variance spheres), an extension not evaluated in prior mode-connectivity work.
Reasonably transparent hyperparameter and configuration reporting (extensive tables) that aids reproducibility for those willing to reimplement the pipeline.
weaknesses: The claimed 'generality' is undercut by the fact that success is reported to hinge almost entirely on architecture-specific, manually engineered layer ordering/phasing (Appendix F shows bespoke multi-phase schedules per model). This is effectively a hand-tuned curriculum for each new architecture rather than a general-purpose algorithm, which weakens the central claim of broad applicability with 'appropriate search hyperparameters.'

Very high computational cost: Table 8 reports the equivalent of up to hundreds of thousands of training epochs and dozens of hours of GPU time per single mode-connection instance, far exceeding standard training cost; this raises serious questions about the practical utility of the method relative to simply retraining a model, and is not adequately discussed as a limitation relative to significance claims.

The theoretical apparatus (variance spheres, Equations 3–6, the 'proof' in Appendix M) is largely a restatement of the fact that squared L2 norm is proportional to variance under a zero-mean assumption; it does not provide non-trivial theoretical justification for why the algorithm should work, and the empirical justification for Equation 5 (mean ≈ 0) is only approximate and not rigorously bounded.

No direct quantitative comparison against the most closely related prior method, layer-wise linear mode connectivity (Adilova et al., 2024), which the authors explicitly credit as the mechanism underlying their gains; the comparison table (Table 1) only includes FGE and AutoNEB, leaving the actual novelty/advantage over the directly relevant baseline unquantified.

The method does not guarantee low test loss even when training loss is low (explicitly acknowledged for ResNet18), which undermines the interpretation of the discovered paths as genuinely connecting 'low-loss' generalizing solutions rather than just fitting the training set locally.

The speculative 'full path-connectedness of SGD basins' hypothesis in the Discussion is presented with some emphasis despite the authors' own admission that no theoretical framework supports it and evidence is limited to a handful of CIFAR-scale architectures; broader claims about the loss landscape geometry are not well supported by the narrow experimental scope (CIFAR10/100 and small ImageNet10 subsets only, no large-scale ImageNet results).

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy (P vs. θ, multiple algorithms with many hyperparameters: step_a, step_c, step_f, r, phase schedules), which combined with the need for per-model manual configuration reduces accessibility and reproducibility for a general reader despite the large appendix.

strengths: Extensive empirical breadth: the algorithm is tested on a wide and modern range of architectures (ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, CCT) across CIFAR10/100 and ImageNet10, going well beyond the narrow architecture set used in prior mode-connectivity work.

Careful and valuable critical re-examination of prior baselines: the paper identifies a concrete seeding bug in the released FGE code (Appendix C) showing the reported 'independently trained' modes are actually near-duplicates, and empirically documents the inconsistency of AutoNEB across repeated runs (loss ranging 0.5-1.5). This is a genuine, verifiable contribution to the literature's understanding of what these baselines actually measure.

The method is evaluated with substantial repetition (>=10 runs per architecture) and the resulting low variance in loss/accuracy trajectories (Fig. 2-3) supports the claimed reproducibility, which is a property explicitly absent from prior methods.

The extension to connecting modes across different training hyperparameters (different 'variance spheres') is a novel and useful capability not addressed by prior connectivity methods, demonstrated concretely for DLA/ResNet18/CCT7 (Fig. 4, Appendix G).

High transparency and reproducibility effort: very detailed hyperparameter tables (Appendix F), ablations isolating each algorithmic component (variance correction, retraining, layer-wise moves; Appendix I), and continuity checks via linear interpolation between successive path points (Fig. 5, Appendix H).
weaknesses: The algorithm's applicability across architectures relies on extensive, manually engineered per-architecture layer orderings and multi-phase schedules (Table 4 shows 20+ hand-specified phases for DLA, 6-9 for ResNet18/CCT7). While the paper states the 'Follow Data Flow' heuristic generalizes this, the actual configurations still appear to require substantial architecture-specific tuning, which weakens the claim of a broadly 'generalizable' algorithm and raises questions about the effort needed to apply LLPF to a genuinely new architecture not covered here.

The method does not guarantee low test loss/accuracy along the path (explicitly acknowledged for ResNet18, Fig. 2 third row), which is an important caveat since generalization along the path is often part of what makes mode connectivity meaningful; this somewhat undercuts the practical significance of the 'low-loss path' claims.

Theoretical grounding is thin: the central approximations (near-zero mean, variance-sphere proximity of independently trained modes) are justified only empirically on a handful of architectures/datasets (Appendix A-B), and the 'proof' in Appendix M is a trivial algebraic identity rather than a substantive theoretical result. The broader discussion (Section 6) speculates about full path-connectedness of SGD basins without any supporting theory, which is a fairly strong conjecture to raise from limited empirical evidence.

Computational cost is very high (21-45 GPU-hours per single mode pair per architecture, Table 8), which may limit the practical utility of LLPF as a tool for 'systematically navigating' the loss landscape, contrary to the efficiency framing in the introduction.

Comparisons to baselines in Table 1 mix different backbone variants (ResNet20 for AutoNEB vs. ResNet18 for LLPF) and different loss scales taken partly from original papers and partly from the authors' own reproduction, making the head-to-head numeric comparison somewhat apples-to-oranges despite the qualitative point being valid.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not engage with any specific limitations or potential misuses of the work (e.g., compute cost, scalability to large-scale models/ImageNet), and the paper does not test on full ImageNet or larger contemporary models (e.g., ViT-scale transformers), leaving open how well the layer-wise approach scales.
